en: I have lost him to the dogs;
My precious Manas, take me with you!
Leopard, you were the one who gathered gold;
I am the one who suffers for it.
You were the one who gathered silver;
The six villains enjoyed its benefits,
I am the one who bears its grief.
Suffering misery, I sank beneath it;
My bright day turned to night.
O God, I prepared to leave for my own kin.
My Kara-Buura, my Chatkal,
Farewell, you countless Kyrgyz,
All of you lying at your ease!
In red dresses, with slender waists,
Farewell, your daughters!
In black felt hats and blue coats,
Farewell, my dear Kyrgyz!
With braid ornaments at their hips and broad hair pendants,
May your young wives remain safe!
More rice than dark grain,
More silver than tin,
More foxes than gray hares,
Much wealth heaped beside the doorway.
Dear people, you wore fox and sable furs;
What has happened will never be forgotten.
All my gold has turned to stone;
The six villains have become the people's chiefs.
The forty companions the Bloodstained One left behind
Have proved enemies in their deeds.
Drawing bows, sending arrows like rain,
They have tormented me;
They have roused me fully from sleep;
They have raided my horses like this;
They have utterly silenced my laughter;
They have utterly exhausted my wealth.
While my sovereign lived,
I gathered silk as though it were felt.
The forty companions the hero left behind
Did not value me afterward.
While my Magnanimous One lived,
I gathered precious things as though they were felt.
We were friends bound beyond the grave,
Yet afterward the forty companions
Raided my encampment.
My gold was worth less than coal;
The sons of the junior wife
Grew fat on wrecking my encampment.
My silver was worth less than coal;
The sons of the junior wife
Grew fat on plundering my court.”
Kanykey wept and cried aloud.
How could your sister-in-law spare herself?
The noble khan Almambet's Syr Barang—
(She could not find Manas's Akkelte)—
She used it as a walking stick, leaning on it.
Your accomplished, fierce sister-in-law
Now felt what it was to be a widow.
Which no bullet pierced when worn in battle—
She could not find the Ak-Olpok;
The fine white cloth coat left by Manas,
She put that fine white cloth coat on.
How could your noble sister-in-law spare herself?
The battle-axe left by Manas,
She leaned upon that battle-axe.
She gathered courage and girded her waist.
Parted from her Bloodstained One,
She wept in grief, her eyes glistening.
Wounded in many places,
She walked in sorrow, her misery seething.
The flesh at her collarbone was torn apart;
Blood flowing from her side
Poured from the hem of her dress.
Not even half a grain of wheat remained;
They had ravaged everything.
They had not left even a shaggy yearling colt;
They had brought her to utter ruin like this.
Not a cord remained for a wrist-strap,
Not a dog remained to stir and bark,
Not a crow flew cawing,
Not a raven flew croaking.
There was no one to look after her.
O God, there was nothing to snatch a bite of.
The wide world had grown narrow.
Kanykey, sovereign of the world,
Parted from her Magnanimous One,
Was now to wander in humiliation.
Yesterday, coughing harshly,
Lifting his head from the pillow,
Turning his white neck,
Her betrothed, her gray-maned wolf,
While he lay gravely ill,
Had held her hand and spoken:
“My fierce one, seek your own kin,” he had said.
When the prince's eyes had closed forever,
“O God, what shall I do staying here?
Let me go to my own kin, Temir Khan.
My kinsmen have become my enemies.
O God, my bitterness remains within me.
Rather than suffer at the hands of those near me,
Let me endure hardship far away.
The banner fastened to the spear,
The gift left by the Magnanimous One,
Let me carry it away, even to my death.
If I stand here wailing,
There is no understanding kinsman either.
O God, what inheritance can I claim?
Taking the orphan away,
Rather than this, O God,
Let me wander off to Bukhara!
While I lament Talas, crying aloud,
While I stand sobbing and weeping,
Whose head was wrapped in sacred willow,
Whose feet were propped against rows of gold,
Who wore a cap of gray lynx fur,
Who wielded a mottled blue shield,
Who pondered the words of the Quran's primer,
Who rinsed his mouth with honey,
A bringer of good fortune when sent ahead,
Like a vast army when following behind,
Who found the right words in a sudden crisis,
Who found a way to see in darkness,
Who would find a way for me—
My elder Bakay is not here!
It was a night of darkened moon;
For your fierce mother, the she-wolf,
It was a day for bearing torment.
Who rode the horse Aysarala,
Who carried a spear without a tassel,
Who wore a bare sword at his side—
If God had to take the Magnanimous One,
If only Almambet, his sworn brother, had remained!
While Almambet stood watching,
Let them try to inflict this humiliation!
Let the dogs try to plunder my court then!
Or that tall man with broad shoulders,
That tempered blade of black steel,
If only he stood beside me!
If only Khan Baltay's Chubak were here!
Whom no man had strength to overcome in wrestling,
Whom even a wolf's teeth could not pierce,
Yraman's son, the Singer—
Whose drawstring was tasseled, with forty knots,
He has vanished from my sight;
Alas, he has not come near me.
Oh, the deep pit dug for me!
Oh, my seething misery!
My brow's ill fortune,
My scant share of happiness!
Light on a horse, fit for a colt,
Never resting on his elbow,
Never snatching even a brief sleep,
Sleepless, watchful on the road—
Ulak Khan's Syrgak,
If that nest-mate stood beside me,
How could such a fate befall
This bereaved woman?
For me, fierce Kanykey,
Only the mountains remain to lean on.
My elder father-in-law, that swine of a khan, has joined the accusers.
His horse Telkyzyl stood well fed,
Yet when the dogs attacked all around,
That keen warrior Ajybay was absent.
Your father's grave, forty companions!
If only I had seen one benefit from them!
All forty were dogs from forty different places.
For forty swine from forty places,
Making forty coats of mail,
I struggled and suffered torment.
Drawing bows, sending arrows like rain,
Firing shots like hail,
You became a distant mountain for me to cross;
Afterward you became my very enemies.
Alas, what a day! My soul's beloved,
Who died along with my Bloodstained One—
My light, Koyonaaly of yesterday!
With my wings broken,
Do you see me leaving in lament?
Parted from my bloodstained heroes,
While I stand sobbing and weeping,
O God, what desire can I fulfill?
My companion in sorrow will not rise and return;
What use is all this wailing?
Firmly girding my unyielding waist,
Let me wander off to Bukhara!”
Saying these words then,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Took her lovely long, thick braid,
And bound it snugly on her crown.
The old fur cap left by Prince Manas,
Dear Kanykey
Set snugly on her head.
With golden collar and copper sleeves,
The double mail, its rings like larks' eyes,
She put on over her clothes.
The Gray Belt that descended from heaven,
The belt that was leopard Manas's friend,
She fastened snugly around her waist.
The countless possessions left by Manas,
Your sister-in-law was ready to scatter;
To the city of her own kin, Temir Khan,
Your sister-in-law was ready to flee.
She walked shrieking and crying aloud.
The world of truth had descended upon her;
She offered heartfelt supplications,
Straining her fly-like little soul,
Turning all she grasped to embers,
Raising her great head as a banner,
Making herself, a woman, into a warrior.
Her eyes glistened as she cried;
The one on whom she truly rested her hope
Was Semetey, for whom she girded her waist.
Every straight road
Had become a straight, dark road.
Let Kanykey remain there a moment,
Having suffered violence from her kin,
Humiliated then and there.
Unable to cross the ridge on foot,
Your heroic mother Kanykey,
Unable to reach the appointed place,
Exhausted, weeping, worn out,
Through wide Talas's Uyurulmo—
Along Uyurulmo she traveled.
How could your mother spare herself?
Distraught in her misfortune, weeping and crying,
At the spur where the mountain ended,
Skirting Kara-Kyr,
At Kara-Kyr's projecting point,
On the spur that swept back,
There was Khan Manas's little enclosure;
She entered the enclosure, crying aloud.
“My hero, give me your support,” she said,
And went toward it sobbing.
When she approached the mausoleum,
If you ask what she looked like,
Upon her great dark head,
Your mother's bloody face was torn.
When she saw the little enclosure,
Your mother's strength deserted her.
From her radiant white face, broad as a platter,
Blood ran like water in a ditch.
Dear Kanykey,
Half senseless, staggering along,
The blood from both her cheeks
Streaming down her collarbone, said:
“Shall I reach Bukhara safely?
My mighty prince, my leopard,
Must I leave you here?
Farewell, Kara-Kol and Kosh-Ashuu!
Farewell, remain in peace!
Until I come back again,
Until I return to see the mausoleum,
Honored Manas, rest in peace!
Rest in peace, my Talas;
Rest safely, my Manas,
My cave of hidden treasure!
